source: Li et al. (2024) Confidence Matters: Revisiting Intrinsic Self-Correction Capabilities of LLMs (If-or-Else prompt)
finding: Telling the model to keep its answer unless it is not very confident (If-or-Else, IoE) removed most of the loss that Huang's 'find problems' prompt causes. Critique hurts confident answers and helps unconfident ones.
numbers: GSM8K-100, gpt-3.5-turbo-1106, T=0: standard 75.6%, critical prompt 72.4%. Confident set (87 of 100): 82.75% to 77.35% under critique. Unconfident set (13): 27.69% to 39.23%. Table 5 averages over GSM8K, SVAMP, HotpotQA, Sports, LLC: GPT-3.5-0613 standard 70.3, critical 66.1, IoE 73.0, IoE+Decision 73.7. GPT-4: 85.1, 82.5, 86.6, 86.9. Mistral-Medium: 74.8, 57.7, 75.2, 75.3. GPT-4 GSM8K 92.5 / 88.4 / 93.4. Confidence by 10-run consistency raised GSM8K-100 from 75.6 to 77.09; one-trial self-assessed confidence gave 75 to 80.
quote: Review your previous answer. If you are very confident about your answer, maintain your answer. Otherwise, update your answer.
limits: Single run per cell, no error bars; gains over the standard prompt are +1.5 (GPT-4) to +3.4 (GPT-3.5) points on a 5-set average and shrink as the model gets stronger. Benchmarks of 100 to 1,319 items. The Figure 4 flip percentages were unreadable in the PDF text, so the exact right-to-wrong fall is not extracted; the paper says right-to-wrong fell clearly vs the critical prompt (GPT-3.5-1106, GSM8K and SVAMP). The 'decision' stage needs a second sample.
agent_relevance: Supports a keep-unless-sure wording in the S5 check. Gap 8 is partly answered: the prompt mostly cancels Huang's loss but adds only about 1 to 3 points over doing nothing. Needs a retest on a reasoning model.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: With a model fine-tuned to revise, N sequential revisions beat N parallel samples at the same generation count, and the best mix of the two beats best-of-N with up to 4x less compute. Prompted revision was not used because it is ineffective.
numbers: PaLM 2-S* on MATH. Fine-tuned revision model turns about 38% of correct answers into wrong ones if used naively. Selecting with a verifier or sequential majority vote over the chain fixes this. Easy questions do best with an all-sequential budget; hard ones need a balance of sequential and parallel. Up to 4x less test-time compute than parallel best-of-N.
quote: Simply prompting existing LLMs to correct their own mistakes tends to be largely ineffective for obtaining performance improvements on reasoning problems
limits: The revision model was trained for this (capability-specific fine-tuning was 'necessary'). 2023-era PaLM 2, not a long-CoT reasoning model. The verifier is a trained PRM/ORM, so this is not intrinsic. Only partly answers gap 1.
agent_relevance: Equal-compute evidence that a revise loop can beat resampling exists, but only with trained revision and a selector. For a prompt-only agent, expect to need a selector (vote or check) over the chain, and a difficulty-dependent split. Counterpart of K16.

source: Stroebl, Kapoor, Narayanan (2024; v3 2026) The Limits of Inference Scaling Through Resampling
finding: When the checker is imperfect (unit tests with limited coverage), resampling until a pass has a hard ceiling set by the false-positive rate. Weak models have more false positives. With a cost for a false pass, the best number of tries is small.
numbers: HumanEval+ and MBPP+ used as hidden truth; original HumanEval/MBPP tests as the verifier. 200 samples per task on HumanEval+ (1,000 for Command Light), 50 on MBPP+. False-positive rate falls linearly as single-sample accuracy rises (Command, GPT-4o, Llama-3.1 families). At cost-benefit ratio 4 the best K is about 5 for all four models; at higher ratios the best K can be 0. False-positive rate rises with K for Llama-3.1-70B, slowly for Code Llama and Command.
quote: no amount of inference scaling of weaker models can enable them to match the single-sample accuracy of a sufficiently strong model
limits: Coding tasks with sparse tests only. The reason Llama-3.1-70B differs from Code Llama in how fast false positives grow is unexplained. Tests are an outside checker, not a model check.
agent_relevance: Direct answer to gap 5: a checker that can be wrong sets a ceiling and a false pass has a price. S5 should cap retries (about 5) and weight a pass by test coverage; never treat a model-written test pass as proof.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Prompted models can find the first wrong step in a math solution, but a reasoning-trained model does it far better than a normal chat model. QwQ-32B-Preview matches GPT-4o; o1-mini is far ahead.
numbers: 3,400 test cases over GSM8K, MATH, OlympiadBench, Omni-MATH. Score is the F1 of accuracy on erroneous and correct samples. Average F1: o1-mini 87.9, GPT-4o-0806 61.9. o1-mini per set about 93.2 (GSM8K), 88.9 (MATH), 87.2 (Olympiad), 82.4 (Omni). Open models: majority vote of 8 samples; GPT-4o greedy; o1-mini single sample. Open PRMs trained on PRM800K do worse than prompted critics on the harder sets.
limits: Math only; the table in the text extraction was partly scrambled, so only the Figure 1 averages and the o1-mini row are trusted. Human-labelled error steps. Models are late 2024; 2025-26 models not tested in this paper. Locating an error is not the same as fixing it.
agent_relevance: Answers the second half of gap 6: a cheap first-wrong-step locator is feasible with a reasoning model (F1 88) but not with a plain chat model (F1 62). A locate step needs the strong model; whether locate-then-fix beats one-shot critique at equal tokens is still untested.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Understanding the Dark Side of LLMs' Intrinsic Self-Correction
finding: A neutral 'are you sure, think again' round made models change correct answers on every task tested, including o1-mini, 4o, DeepSeek V3 and R1. In a 10-round chat most answers flip many times. Re-attaching the original question at the end of the refinement prompt cut the damage.
numbers: BoolQ 3,270 questions; ALFWorld 134; HotPotQA 100; HumanEval 161. Accuracy fell after feedback+refinement for all four tasks. Llama-3.1-8B: -20.4 points, 58.8% of correct answers overturned. GPT-3.5-turbo: 81.3% of answers changed more than 6 times in 10 rounds. Question repeating: ACC +3.2 to +4.9, overturn rate -5.3 to -10.9 points. SFT on 4 (Llama) or 10 (GPT) examples also reduced overturning and generalised to other tasks. o1-mini in ALFWorld: 15.4 'think' loops in failed runs vs 5.3 in normal runs.
limits: Several table cells were garbled in extraction, so per-model Table 1/2 numbers beyond the Llama-3.1-8B headline are not quoted. Refinement was applied even when the first answer was right (no oracle), which is the stress case. Prompts are 'are you sure' style, not a cheap structured check.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 7: supports a hard cap of 1 round and putting the original question in the last position of every check prompt. Add to S5: restate the task last.

source: Dip, Zhou, Zhang (2026) Think Again or Think Longer? Selective Verification for Budget-Aware Reasoning (SEVRA)
finding: Best direct equal-token test found for gap 1. On a small reasoning model, one verification pass fixed truncated or slipped answers, but simply giving the first solve a larger token budget matched the best verification result with fewer tokens.
numbers: Frozen Qwen3-4B. MATH500: base with 4,096-token limit 59.0; always continue 72.0 (3.6% harmful flips); always active-verify 75.5 (2.2% flips, 7,064 total tokens); selective verify 76.3 (1.0% flips, 8,125 tokens, 26.8% fewer action tokens than always verify; accuracy gain over always verify not significant, p=.103; flip cut significant, p<.001); long base with 8,192-token limit 76.0 using 5,124 tokens (28% fewer total tokens, no second call). GSM8K: base 93.40; always verify 93.40 (1,752 action tokens, 1.25% flips); selective 94.47 (verifies 3.0%, 0 flips); long base 94.54 (selective minus long: -0.08, CI [-0.91, 0.80]). CommonsenseQA: base about 76.49, always verify 72.32 (-4.17, 5.94% flips); self-consistency@5 +1.88 points (CI [0.66, 3.11]) at about 5x tokens.
limits: One small model (Qwen3-4B), one solver family, frozen; 45.4% of MATH500 first attempts were truncated at 4,096 tokens, so much of the 'fix' is finishing cut-off work; only 2.9% truncated on GSM8K. Not a test of semantic error detection. The CommonsenseQA base value is inferred from the stated deltas because the table text was scrambled.
agent_relevance: Core answer to gap 1: for a reasoning model, tune the first-solve budget first; a check call is worth its tokens only when auditing or regression control is needed, and then it should be gated. Do not assume revise beats think-longer.

source: Bilal et al. (2026) Refining Over Resampling: Test-Time Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning
finding: N=8 rollouts each refined D=4 times by self-critique and self-correction, then majority vote, beat greedy, Maj@8, reward-model best-of-8, beam and lookahead on five math sets for small non-reasoning models. The gain is bigger for weaker models.
numbers: Averages over AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH500. Ours 44.59 (one model), 25.67 (Qwen2.5-1.5B), 29.46, 24.92 (the other two of Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Ministral-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, row order scrambled). Qwen2.5-1.5B: Maj@8 13.21, RM@8 14.95, ours 25.67 (+17 TFLOP-normalised gain). The 44.59 model: greedy 36.33; vs RM@8 only +2.36. Extra compute used over baselines runs from 630 to 3,385 TFLOPs. Critic ablation (corrector sees trace only vs full critique) Qwen2.5-1.5B: MATH500 55.6 to 58.0, AMC 27.5 to 32.5, AIME25 0.0 to 6.67. Temperature 0.7, N=8, D=4.
limits: Not equal compute: the refine method spends the extra TFLOPs listed, while Maj@8 and RM@8 get fewer. Non-reasoning models (Qwen2.5 family, LLaMA-3.1-8B). Voting after refinement may be doing the work, since the paper admits single corrections are noisy. Single run on 30-problem sets (AIME) means big variance. Table rows were scrambled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Shows refine-then-vote is better than vote alone for weak models, but it does not answer gap 1 for a long-CoT model, and the compute is not matched. Treat as a hint for 'vote over checked drafts', not as proof.

source: Lin et al. (2026) When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling
finding: For large reasoning models (Qwen3 family), routing by answer disagreement (consistent: accept; moderate: vote; high: rewrite the problem and re-solve) beats voting alone at matched sample counts. Rewriting works when the problem hides a condition, and hurts when a short clear problem gets over-compressed.
numbers: Qwen3-8B, 7 math benchmarks, average: single 61.3 (+-0.71), majority 68.9 (+-0.26), best-of-N 63.4, DV 67.3, SCoP 67.4, routing 75.8 (+-0.43). Qwen3-4B: single 60.4, majority 68.0. Budgets matched at 4 and 8 samples (8 samples = 3 iterations of 2 samples plus a rewrite-and-rethink step). Error classes fixed by rewrite: hidden-information errors; not fixed: answer-format, context-loss, calculation errors; harmed: over-compression of short questions.
limits: Math only; rewriting is a re-presentation of the question, not a check of a draft. Spread reported but seed count not stated in the extracted text. Compares to voting, not to a revise-the-draft step.
agent_relevance: Relevant to gaps 1 and 2: re-presenting the problem fresh (instead of showing the old draft) helped a reasoning model at matched samples. Suggests an S5 variant: re-solve from a restated task rather than critique the draft. Not a test of the attribution framing.

source: Stav, Berlowitz, Orner, Kraus (2026) When Does Intrinsic Self-Correction Help? A Task-Sensitive Analysis
finding: Temperature-0 intrinsic revision on five 2025-26 models gave large gains on SAT (easy to verify), moderate on BBEH, small and mixed on HLE, and a model-specific loss on Codenames. Wrong-to-correct (W2C) and correct-to-wrong (C2W) rates are reported per model.
numbers: Accuracy base to SC. SAT: Mistral Large 2512 34.62 to 64.96; Claude Haiku 4.5 75.64 to 93.59; DeepSeek V3.1 78.63 to 92.74; Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite 60.68 to 82.91; Gemini 3 Pro 97.0 to 100. BBEH non-choice: Mistral 17.04 to 25.67; Haiku 28.75 to 31.92; DeepSeek 35.34 to 46.99; Gemini Pro 80.88 to 82.30. HLE text choice: Mistral 9.5 to 26.5; Haiku 11.0 to 34.5; Gemini 2.5 Pro 34.16 to 35.40. W2C/C2W (percent of all items): SAT Mistral 32.5/2.1, Haiku 17.9/0.0, DeepSeek 14.5/0.4; BBEH non-choice DeepSeek 14.1/2.4, Haiku 9.9/6.8; HLE Haiku 11.0/8.5, Gemini Pro 10.56/9.32; C2W reached 13.25% on BBEH/HLE for some models. Haiku changed its Codenames clue in about 99% of turns and lost accuracy (0.990 to 0.889).
limits: Temperature 0, one run per cell, McNemar for significance; no seeds or error bars. The SC prompt is a plain 'revisit' (two-step) or critique-then-revise (three-step) and uses extra calls, so it is not matched to a resample baseline. The Gemini Pro column mixes Gemini 3 Pro and 2.5 Pro. Weak models' base answers may have been truncated or badly formatted, which a second pass fixes.
agent_relevance: Best current answer to gaps 3 and 4: on SAT-like (checkable) tasks the right-to-wrong rate is near zero and fixes are large; on open reasoning the ratio is close to even for the strongest model (HLE Gemini Pro 10.6 vs 9.3). Use S5 hard only where a check is cheap and sound; otherwise gate.

source: Yin, Ken, Stremmel (2026) Denoising Iterative Self-Correction (DISC): Structured Verification Loops for Reliable LLM Reasoning
finding: A verify, judge, correct loop with a binary judge gate that blocks rewrites beat Chain-of-Verification and Self-Refine on precision (improvements per degradation) and, mostly, on accuracy. Removing the gate lowers the improvement-to-degradation ratio 2 to 4 times.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake (traces start at 15% correct), N=1,790: Sonnet 4.5 DISC(K=3) 81.6% (1,195 improved, 8 degraded, 149:1), CoVe 58.6 (851/75, 11.3:1), Self-Refine 49.6 (633/21, 30.1:1). GPT-4o: DISC 49.9, CoVe 62.0, Self-Refine 27.6 (289/57). HotpotQA N=7,405 F1: Sonnet 65.1 to 80.4 (DISC), 80.0 (CoVe), 77.8 (SR); GPT-4o 75.0 to 77.9 (DISC), 73.9 (CoVe), 74.6 (SR). GPQA Diamond N=198, gpt-5.2: 75.3 to 79.3 (DISC, 18 improved/10 degraded), CoVe 69.7 (17/28), SR 75.3 (13/13). Bootstrap 95% CIs reported. Ablation: no gate lowers I:D 2 to 4x; Sonnet BBM Dyck 50.8 vs 47.1 without gate (221/8 vs 222/31). Mean calls per example: DISC 9.5 to 15.9, CoVe 6.9 to 10.1, Self-Refine 1.0 to 2.8.
limits: BBM initial accuracy of 15% leaves few correct answers to break, which flatters degradation counts. DISC uses far more calls than Self-Refine, so no equal-call comparison. Preprint, one lab, API content-policy filters removed some items. On GPT-4o HotpotQA the gate lost 88 EM.
agent_relevance: Supports a gated check (a judge says MISTAKE or NO_MISTAKE before any rewrite) for S5, and K of about 3 at most. Partial answer to gaps 7 and 8.

source: Yin et al. (2026) DISC, cross-model and iteration-budget experiments (same paper as d10)
finding: A checker that is a different, stronger model fixes far more than the same model checking itself, and both the verifier and the judge must be strong. Extra iterations plateau after 3 and do not compound damage when a gate is present.
numbers: GPQA Diamond, 198 questions, gpt-4.1-nano (weak) vs gpt-5.2 (strong). All-nano: 54.0 to 54.0 (0 improved). Strong judge only: 55.6 (+3 net). Strong verifier only: 54.3 (0 net). Strong verifier and judge on nano outputs: 54.3 to 71.6 (51 improved, 17 degraded, +34 net). All gpt-5.2 (self-check): 75.3 to 79.3 (+8 net). gpt-5.2 verifier flagged 51 errors in nano's outputs vs 18 in its own; judge precision 71.3% / recall 85.6% on nano outputs vs 62.0% / 63.3% on its own. Nano judge said NO_MISTAKE on all 90 wrong answers although the evidence contradicted the answer in 89 of 90. Iteration sweep K=1,2,3,5,7,8: net +22 at K=1, +34 at K=3 (I:D 2.0 to 3.0), +33 at K=5, +35 at K=8; degradation 23 at K=1, 17 at K=3, 16 at K=7-8; convergence 46.5% at K=1, 78.7% at K=3, 90.4% at K=8; K=3 gets 97% of max net gain.
limits: Single question set (GPQA Diamond, 198 items), CIs overlap on small differences. 'Different model' confounds capability with independence from the generator's blind spots; the stronger model also simply knows more. Not a pure test of attribution.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence for gap 2: independence of the checker from the generator matters (+34 vs +8 net), but a scaffold with one model cannot buy a stronger checker. Use as a reason to give the check a fresh context with the draft presented as someone else's. Round cap: 3 with a gate; without a gate expect damage.

source: Yin et al. (2026) DISC per-task tables on BIG-Bench Mistake, Chain-of-Verification baseline (same paper as d10)
finding: Chain-of-Verification (item-by-item checks, one pass) does not carry over cleanly to multi-step reasoning: on recomputable tasks it breaks many correct answers for one model, while a gated version does not.
numbers: Sonnet 4.5, final accuracy / degradation of originally correct answers. Multistep Arithmetic: DISC 98.3 / 0%, CoVe 43.7 / 28.9%, Self-Refine 15.3 / 4.4%. Word Sorting: DISC 89.6, CoVe 61.1 / 35.6%, SR 53.2 / 9.1%. Dyck Languages (n=592): DISC 50.8 / 9.1%, CoVe 24.5 / 51.1%, SR 15.0 / 17.0%. Tracking Shuffled Objects: all 99 to 100. GPT-4o: multistep arithmetic DISC 54.0, CoVe 95.0, SR 14.0; Dyck 18.9 / 10.8 / 6.8 with CoVe degrading 44.3%.
limits: CoVe is re-implemented by the DISC authors (factored variant, few-shot prompts) and its prompts differ from DISC's; a prompt-swap ablation (DISC prompts in CoVe's architecture on GPQA) gave 67.2 vs native CoVe 69.7. The result is mixed by model: GPT-4o CoVe is best on arithmetic (95.0).
agent_relevance: Gap 9: item-by-item checking in isolation can work on recomputable arithmetic for one model and break answers for another, so it does not transfer reliably without a gate. Do not use bare CoVe for reasoning claims; add a keep/change judgment.

source: Chen, Lin, Scharli, Zhou (2023/2024) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: With unit tests as the check, one debugging turn gives most of the gain and a debug step can beat drawing many more samples. Without execution, the gain mostly disappears or turns negative on some models.
numbers: MBPP: Codex 61.4 baseline, 68.2 simple feedback, 69.4 unit-test (UT) feedback, 70.8 UT + trace; GPT-3.5 67.6 to 72.2 (UT); GPT-4 72.8 to 80.6 (UT). TransCoder: Codex 80.4 to 91.6 (UT); GPT-4 77.3 to 88.8 (UT), 90.4 best variant. Spider (no tests): Codex 81.3 to 84.1 with explanation; GPT-4 73.2 to 73.6. Without execution on MBPP: Codex simple 57.6 (below baseline 61.4), GPT-3.5 68.2, GPT-4 76.0. Sample efficiency (Spider, Codex): greedy + debug matches baseline at 16 samples; debug from 8 samples beats 32 samples; accuracy gain after turn 1 within 0.1%.
limits: Old models (Codex, GPT-3.5, early GPT-4), few-shot prompts, some tests visible in the prompt. Table cell labels were slightly scrambled in extraction; the MBPP and TransCoder UT assignments above follow row order. Sample-efficiency is about execution-based comparisons, not equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 anchor: for code with real tests, check-and-fix beats best-of-n at similar or smaller sample counts, and one turn is enough (also supports a gap 7 cap of 1). Without a sound check the effect is lost.

source: Zhao, Awasthi, Gollapudi (2025) Sample, Scrutinize and Scale: Effective Inference-Time Search by Scaling Verification
finding: Sampling 200 answers and having the same model self-verify each one (Verification@200) beat 200-sample majority vote on all four reasoning sets for Gemini 1.5 Pro and passed o1-Preview. The authors also found that frontier models verify poorly out of the box.
numbers: Gemini 1.5 Pro. AIME: pass@1 1/15; Consistency@200 4/15; Consistency@1,000 3/15; Verification@200 8/15; o1-Preview 7/15. MATH (500): 426; 460; 460; 467; 428. LiveBench Math (200): 104; 118; 120; 135; 131. LiveBench Reasoning (140): 63; 75; 73; 97; 95. Sampling a larger pool improved verification accuracy ('implicit scaling'). Comparing across responses helps locate errors; chain-of-thought outputs are harder to verify.
quote: frontier models demonstrate remarkably weak out-of-box verification capabilities
limits: Single run per cell (stated: 'due to the high expense'); AIME has 15 questions. Non-reasoning model; 200 samples times verification calls is a huge budget. The o1-preview API result they measured was 26% on AIME, not the 44% public figure.
agent_relevance: For gaps 1 and 4: at large budgets, verify-then-select over many drafts beats plain voting, but this is a many-sample regime, not a single check on a single draft. Compare across drafts; do not check one draft alone.

source: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han, Zhang (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
finding: Review of prior self-correction work: no prior work shows successful prompted self-correction in general tasks under fair settings. It works when the task has an exceptionally easy check (decomposable answers), when a reliable external signal exists, and with large-scale fine-tuning.
numbers: Three findings from the abstract: (1) no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs except in tasks exceptionally suited to it; (2) self-correction works well where reliable external feedback exists; (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables it. Table 4 lists unfair settings: oracle information (RCI uses ground-truth answers and skips correct ones; Reflexion uses oracle signals) and weak initial prompts. Table 6: most fine-tuning methods need large training sets. CoVe given as an example of a decomposable task (name politicians born in NY).
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except for studies in tasks that are exceptionally suited for self-correction
limits: Survey of work up to mid-2024; covers non-reasoning models. The fine-tuning claim rests on trained methods (SCoRe, RISE) with their own caveats (K17).
agent_relevance: Gaps 10 and 4: a fair prompt-only win has not been shown in general tasks, so S5 should rely on outside checks or decomposable claims. Task list for S5: decomposable lists, recomputable arithmetic, tests.

source: Ma et al. (2025) S2R: Teaching LLMs to Self-verify and Self-correct via Reinforcement Learning
finding: Behaviour-initialising SFT on only 3.1k self-verify/self-correct samples, then RL, raised a 7B math model strongly, but plain long-CoT SFT of similar size reached nearly the same score. So the gain is mostly from training, and the self-check structure adds a little.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B on MATH500: base 51.0; behaviour-initialised SFT (S2R-BI) 81.6 (abstract); original-solution SFT 58.0; Long-CoT SFT 80.2. RL stages bring the model to about 83 to 84 on MATH500 (rows not cleanly aligned in the text extraction). Same recipe tested on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2-7B-Instruct.
limits: Training method, not a prompt. Row alignment for the RL variants was scrambled in the text; only the abstract number 51.0 to 81.6 and the SFT baselines are quoted. Results are for a math-specialised model; no prompt-only control in the same format is run.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: no prompt-only method matched the trained gain in anything found; the training result (about 30 points) vs prompted self-correction (about 0 or negative) is the gap. Do not plan on dropping external signals for a prompt-only agent.

source: Hassid, Synnaeve, Adi, Schwartz (2025; v2 2026) Don't Overthink it. Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains for Improved LLM Reasoning
finding: For reasoning models, the shortest of several sampled chains is more often right than the longest, and stopping at the first few finished chains and voting (short-m@k) beats full majority voting at lower token cost. Longer thinking is not always better.
numbers: Across four reasoning LLMs and four benchmarks, the shortest chain per question was up to 34.5% more accurate than the longest chain. short-1@k matched or beat majority voting in low-compute settings with up to 40% fewer thinking tokens. short-3@k beat majority voting at all budgets with up to 33% less wall time. Shortest chains were 50% and 67% shorter than random and longest.
limits: Abstract-level numbers; exact per-model tables were not extracted. Selection by length is a heuristic that depends on the model family. Relates to chains, not to a second revise call.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a long reasoning chain is partly a sign of error, so a 'think longer' alternative to a check step needs care. Hints that for reasoning models the cheap controls are early stopping and voting on short chains, not a verify call.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning (MBPP false-positive analysis)
finding: Reflexion with self-written unit tests improved HumanEval but made GPT-4 worse on MBPP Python because the model-written tests passed wrong code too often.
numbers: HumanEval Python: base 0.80, Reflexion 0.91; tests: TP 0.99, FN 0.40, FP 0.01, TN 0.60. MBPP Python: base 0.80, Reflexion 0.77 (about 3 points below no loop; Table 1 lists 80.1 vs 77.1); TP 0.84, FN 0.59, FP 0.16, TN 0.41. MBPP Rust: 0.71 to 0.75 (FP 0.16). The authors give the false-positive rate as 16.3% on MBPP Python vs 1.4% on HumanEval Python.
quote: the false positive test execution rate for MBPP Python is 16.3% while the rate for HumanEval Python is a mere 1.4%
limits: Tests are generated by the same model, so the pass signal can be wrong in both directions: false negatives were also high (FN 0.59 on MBPP), which wastes retries. Few runs; GPT-4 early 2023. The authors argue false negatives are less harmful than false positives because the agent can keep its code.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a false pass ended the loop early and left bugs in; the cost on MBPP was about 3 points below no loop. Put a ceiling on trust in any self-made check, and treat a pass as weak evidence unless the checker is independent.

source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
finding: Models can tell their own text from others' above chance, and the strength of self-preference in judging rises linearly with that self-recognition (fine-tuning to change recognition changes the bias).
numbers: Out of the box all three evaluators (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama 2) beat 50% at telling own output from other sources; GPT-4 73.5% accurate distinguishing itself from two other LLMs and humans. Fine-tuning on 500 examples gave over 90% self-recognition for GPT-3.5 and Llama 2. Linear correlation between self-recognition and self-preference (CNN/DailyMail, XSum).
limits: Summarisation judging, not reasoning checks; 2023 models. Correlation under fine-tuning; control tasks (length, vowel count, readability) used to exclude confounders.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 caution: relabelling a draft as 'another solver's' may be partly seen through if the style gives it away, so any gain from the framing should be tested against a draft rewritten in a neutral style.

source: Tsui (2025, COLM 2026 version) Self-Correction Bench: the Self-Correction Blind Spot (design details re-read)
finding: Re-read of the method: the same error is injected off-policy into either the user message or the assistant turn, so the only cue that differs is the chat-template role header. The author scopes the claim to conversational role, not authorship.
numbers: 14 open non-reasoning models, 64.5% average blind spot; frontier closed models, logic and object-tracking tasks also tested. Mean-difference steering at the last error token gives a 'conversational-role direction'. Cause traced to post-training data: SFT data has near-zero correction sequences; reasoning-model data has far more. Correction markers ('Wait', 'But', 'However', 'No', 'Hold on', 'Alternatively', 'Hmm') activate correction.
quote: we therefore scope our claims to conversational role rather than authorship
limits: Injected errors are off-policy (not the model's own mistakes), apart from one experiment on naturally generated errors. No test of a scaffold, of equal tokens, or of accuracy gain after real revision. Role and turn position cannot be varied apart in this design.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 (design reasoning, not a test): any scaffold that pastes the draft into a new user message already puts it in the 'user' role, which is the favourable condition in this study. A direct A/B of 'your previous answer' (assistant turn) vs 'a solver's answer' (user turn) at equal tokens is still unrun.

source: Petrova, Vejsiu (2026) Spectral Origins of the Self-Correction Blind Spot in Autoregressive Generation
finding: A theory paper that claims the blind spot occurs if and only if a spectral radius of an error-propagation operator is at least one, and fits the 89.3% 'Wait' reduction. Its experiments restate known blind-spot results; no scaffold-level or token-matched test.
numbers: Claims 3.2% RMSE between predicted and measured blind-spot rates across four backbones. Restates Tsui's 64.5% and 89.3%. Summarises Ma et al. (S2R: RL, not SFT, installs self-correction) and Lee et al. (ReVISE: self-refinement can degrade output).
limits: Theoretical, unreviewed preprint; I read the abstract and intro only and did not check the proofs. It fits previously published figures, so it adds no independent test.
agent_relevance: No new evidence for gap 2; listed to avoid re-chasing it.
